title: Acute Anaphylaxis

content.title: Acute Anaphylaxis
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine and Allergy and Immunology

redFlags: Airway swelling, stridor, severe bronchospasm or rapidly worsening breathing
Known mast-cell disorder, severe asthma, beta-blocker use or prior biphasic/refractory anaphylaxis
symptoms: Sudden throat tightness, hoarse voice or difficulty swallowing
Breathlessness, wheeze or persistent cough
Generalised itching, flushing, urticaria or swelling
Dizziness, collapse, cramping abdominal pain or vomiting after a likely exposure
physicalSigns: Stridor, angioedema or respiratory distress
Wheeze, hypoxaemia or reduced air entry
Hypotension, tachycardia, poor perfusion or collapse
Generalised urticaria or flushing, noting that skin signs can be absent

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Predominantly lower-airway obstruction without hypotension, acute skin/mucosal change or a clear multisystem exposure response.
Bradycardia, pallor and rapid improvement supine without urticaria, wheeze or airway swelling.
Angioedema without urticaria, often slower onset and limited response to epinephrine or antihistamine.
Infective syndrome and less immediate exposure relationship, although initial shock management may overlap.

ruleIn.testName: Clinical diagnostic criteria
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Clinical diagnostic criteria — Anaphylaxis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Acute airway, breathing or circulatory compromise with compatible skin/mucosal findings or a likely allergen exposure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must not wait for laboratory confirmation.

ruleIn.testName: Serial serum tryptase when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial serum tryptase when indicated — Systemic mast-cell activation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A rise above the person's baseline in an appropriately timed sample.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Can support later specialist evaluation but a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

ruleOut.testName: Point-of-care glucose
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Point-of-care glucose — Hypoglycaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Glucose is not low enough to explain altered consciousness or collapse.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Rapidly excludes a reversible mimic while resuscitation continues.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram — Primary arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary electrical or ischaemic cause for collapse.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Primary arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Particularly important in older patients, chest pain, severe hypotension or epinephrine-related symptoms.

pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a rapid systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Mast-cell and basophil mediator release causes vasodilation, capillary leak, mucosal oedema and bronchoconstriction, which can progress quickly to airway obstruction, distributive shock and cardiac arrest.
keyMechanisms: IgE-mediated or non-IgE pathways trigger widespread mediator release.
Vasodilation and capillary permeability reduce venous return and blood pressure.
Upper-airway oedema and lower-airway bronchospasm compromise ventilation.
Biphasic recurrence can occur after apparent initial resolution.

clinicalManagement.title: Give intramuscular epinephrine
actions: Administer intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh using the current MOH age/weight dosing protocol.
Repeat at the protocol interval if airway, breathing or circulatory compromise persists.
Do not delay epinephrine for antihistamines, corticosteroids, intravenous access or diagnostic tests.

clinicalManagement.title: Position and support airway and breathing
actions: Lay the patient flat with legs elevated unless respiratory distress requires a supported position; avoid sudden standing or sitting.
Call the resuscitation team, give high-concentration oxygen when indicated and prepare early for a difficult airway.
Use inhaled bronchodilator as an adjunct for persistent bronchospasm, never as a substitute for epinephrine.

clinicalManagement.title: Restore circulation
actions: Establish intravenous or intraosseous access and give rapid isotonic crystalloid with frequent reassessment.
Use continuous monitoring and obtain senior critical-care support for refractory shock.
Intravenous epinephrine infusion is restricted to appropriately monitored settings and experienced clinicians.

clinicalManagement.title: Stop exposure and add adjunctive care
actions: Stop the suspected trigger when this can be done safely, such as halting an infusion.
After stabilisation, use adjunctive antihistamine for persistent skin symptoms according to local policy.
Do not rely on corticosteroids to prevent immediate deterioration or replace observation.

clinicalManagement.title: Observe and plan safe discharge
actions: Use risk-stratified observation, extending monitoring after severe, refractory or high-risk reactions.
Document the suspected trigger and all treatment times.
Provide an emergency plan and allergy referral before discharge.

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange allergy evaluation, ensure the event is recorded in the medicine/allergy record, review auto-injector availability before expiry, and advise immediate emergency care for any recurrent systemic reaction.
mdtReferrals: Allergy and immunology for trigger confirmation and prevention planning
Critical care for refractory airway, breathing or circulatory compromise
Dietitian for confirmed food allergy requiring substantial dietary exclusion
Pharmacy for auto-injector access and technique reinforcement
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid the suspected trigger until specialist assessment clarifies the diagnosis.
Review food, medicine and occupational labels without imposing unnecessary broad restriction.
Encourage the patient to carry medical identification and prescribed rescue devices.
patientEducation: Teach recognition of airway, breathing and circulatory symptoms and the need to use an epinephrine auto-injector without delay when prescribed.
Demonstrate auto-injector technique and use teach-back.
Provide written trigger-avoidance and emergency instructions in the patient's preferred language.
dischargeCriteria: Airway, breathing, circulation and skin/mucosal symptoms have fully resolved for the risk-appropriate observation period.
The patient has access to prescribed rescue medication and can demonstrate its use.
Written precautions, suspected-trigger documentation and specialist follow-up are in place.

specialty: Emergency Medicine and Allergy and Immunology

redFlags: Rapidly worsening pain or systemic illness
symptoms: Abdominal pain possibly migrating to right lower quadrant
Loss of appetite
Nausea or vomiting
Fever
Pain worsened by movement or cough
physicalSigns: Right lower quadrant tenderness
Localized guarding
Pain with movement or cough
Possible fever and tachycardia
Variable findings in pregnancy, older adults, and children

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Possible pregnancy, pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, or instability.
Acute unilateral pelvic pain with supportive adnexal imaging.
Colicky flank-to-groin pain and possible hematuria.
Diarrhea or diffuse symptoms may predominate; serial examination helps distinguish.

ruleIn.testName: Serial focused abdominal examination
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial focused abdominal examination — Appendicitis or peritoneal irritation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistent or evolving focal tenderness, guarding, or movement pain.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clinical course and serial findings support diagnosis.

ruleIn.testName: Ultrasound or CT selected by age, pregnancy, and local protocol
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ultrasound or CT selected by age, pregnancy, and local protocol — Appendicitis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Imaging consistent with inflamed appendix or complication.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Clarifies uncertain presentations and identifies complications.

ruleOut.testName: Urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urinalysis — Urinary infection or calculus
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No findings sufficient to explain symptoms when urinary disease is unlikely.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assesses common mimics but does not independently exclude appendicitis.

ruleOut.testName: Pregnancy test when relevant
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pregnancy test when relevant — Pregnancy-related abdominal pain
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Negative when pregnancy is excluded.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Informs differential, imaging, and gynecologic urgency.

pathophysiology.summary: Appendiceal obstruction and inflammation may progress to ischemia, perforation, abscess, or peritonitis.
keyMechanisms: Luminal obstruction
Appendiceal wall inflammation and distension
Venous congestion and ischemia
Perforation and intra-abdominal infection

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and stabilize
actions: Assess observations, hydration, pain, abdominal findings, and peritonitis/sepsis.
Keep fasting when surgery may be needed.
Provide analgesia, antiemetic treatment, and fluids as clinically indicated.
Escalate immediately to emergency and surgical senior review.
Initiate resuscitation and urgent source-control planning.
branches.condition: Peritonitis, sepsis, or instability

actions: Use serial examination and appropriate laboratory or imaging assessment.
Consult surgery if symptoms persist or worsen.
branches.condition: Stable with uncertain diagnosis

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and arrange definitive care
actions: Consult general surgery for suspected appendicitis or complication.
Select imaging and antimicrobial management per patient factors and local pathway.
Document diagnosis, severity, pregnancy status when relevant, and disposition.
Arrange surgical admission and definitive management planning.
Use antimicrobials when indicated by severity and local protocol.
branches.condition: Confirmed or strongly suspected appendicitis

actions: Assess alternative diagnoses and discharge safety.
Give return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, or weakness.
branches.condition: Appendicitis not supported and patient stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: If discharged, arrange follow-up by working diagnosis and advise immediate return for worsening or persistent symptoms.
mdtReferrals: Radiology for uncertain or complex cases
lifestyleAndDiet: Follow fasting instructions while surgery is considered.
Resume oral intake per treating-team advice.
patientEducation: Explain that symptoms can evolve and reassessment may be needed.
Review warning symptoms requiring immediate return.
dischargeCriteria: Serious surgical and pregnancy-related causes assessed
Stable observations and manageable symptoms
Follow-up or observation plan documented
Immediate return precautions understood

redFlags: Shock, fever with toxicity, or metabolic acidosis
Free air or suspected bowel ischaemia
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Bowel Obstruction, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Diffuse bowel dilation without a mechanical transition; consider medicines and recent illness/surgery.
Diarrhoea and absence of progressive distension may support an alternative.
Pain out of proportion or peritonism requires emergency action.

ruleIn.testName: CBC, electrolytes, renal function and lactate when ischaemia is suspected; pregnancy test where relevant.
ruleIn.modalityTarget: CBC, electrolytes, renal function and lactate when ischaemia is suspected; pregnancy test where relevant. — Acute Bowel Obstruction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A result that supports the working diagnosis or defines its severity, interpreted with the clinical picture and current criteria.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Choose this investigation because it can confirm the suspected process, establish baseline risk, or change the next decision in this case.

ruleIn.testName: Abdominal imaging selected with surgical input to define level, transition, closed loop, ischaemia, or perforation.
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Abdominal imaging selected with surgical input to define level, transition, closed loop, ischaemia, or perforation. — Cause, complication, or risk relevant to Acute Bowel Obstruction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A result that may identify a precipitating factor or complication; interpret in context rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Cause, complication, or risk relevant to Acute Bowel Obstruction
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: This helps detect an important alternative or complication and informs safe monitoring and referral.

ruleOut.testName: Focused evaluation for the leading alternative diagnoses
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused evaluation for the leading alternative diagnoses — Important alternative to Acute Bowel Obstruction
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Findings that lower the likelihood of the selected alternative; a normal result does not exclude every urgent cause.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Important alternative to Acute Bowel Obstruction
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: The differential matters because it changes urgency or treatment and should be actively considered.

ruleOut.testName: Serial clinical reassessment with targeted repeat testing when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial clinical reassessment with targeted repeat testing when indicated — Progression or evolving complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Stable or improving clinical trend without new evidence of the suspected complication.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: A single early assessment may miss an evolving problem; repeat only when it can guide care.

pathophysiology.summary: A mechanical blockage or dysmotility causes proximal dilation and fluid sequestration. A closed-loop obstruction can compromise venous and arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: A mechanical blockage or dysmotility causes proximal dilation and fluid sequestration. A closed-loop obstruction can compromise venous and arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess urgency, stability, and the person’s priorities
actions: Confirm the presenting concern, relevant timeline, baseline function, medicines, allergies, comorbidities, and the patient’s immediate priorities.
Assess the red flags above and use the current local escalation pathway if instability or rapid deterioration is present.
Explain uncertainty and involve the patient or appropriate decision-maker in a way suited to the setting.
Escalate immediately to the responsible senior or emergency team using the local pathway.
Stabilise and investigate in parallel; do not delay time-critical action for routine testing.
branches.condition: A red flag, instability, or rapid deterioration is present

actions: Proceed with focused assessment and shared planning.
Document the threshold for urgent reassessment.
branches.condition: The person is stable for a planned or longitudinal pathway

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first contact and whenever the situation changes

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the working diagnosis and stratify risk
actions: Use the history, examination, and investigations listed above to confirm the likely process and assess important alternatives.
Interpret results using current national/local diagnostic criteria, age, pregnancy status, comorbidity, and prior results.
Record severity, uncertainty, and which findings would change the plan.
Reassess the history and examination and seek senior or specialty advice.
Use targeted additional testing only when its result can change management.
branches.condition: The diagnosis remains uncertain or tests conflict with the clinical picture

actions: Switch to the relevant urgent or specialty pathway.
Communicate the finding and handover responsibility clearly.
branches.condition: A high-risk complication or an alternative diagnosis is identified

clinicalManagement.title: Agree evidence-informed care and address the cause
actions: Use the topic-specific focus in this record to agree immediate and longer-term priorities with the patient.
Select treatment only after checking current local guidance, formulary, contraindications, interactions, organ function, pregnancy considerations, and patient preference.
Treat reversible contributors and address access, communication, cultural, and functional barriers.
Reassess diagnosis, treatment burden, adherence barriers, and alternatives with the responsible specialist.
Document the shared decision and safety-net plan.
branches.condition: Treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or inconsistent with the patient’s goals

actions: Continue the plan with monitoring proportional to risk.
Provide clear instructions for expected course and warning symptoms.
branches.condition: The patient improves on the agreed plan

clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to acuity and current local protocol

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate handover, education, and follow-up
actions: Provide a written plan stating the working diagnosis, key findings, medicines or interventions, monitoring, and who owns each next step.
Use teach-back to check that the patient or caregiver understands warning symptoms, follow-up, and how to obtain help.
Close the loop on pending results, referrals, and screening or prevention actions.
Arrange a higher level of care or supported transfer and send a structured clinical handover.
Confirm transport, caregiver, and communication needs where relevant.
branches.condition: Safe care cannot be delivered in the current setting

actions: Confirm a feasible follow-up date and contact route.
Document when and how the plan should be reviewed or escalated.
branches.condition: The patient is ready for outpatient or continuing care

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before transition and at the agreed review interval

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review the topic-specific focus, patient goals, symptoms and function at an interval matched to risk. Reconcile new results and treatment effects, close referrals, and revisit the plan if the condition, circumstances, or preferences change.
mdtReferrals: Primary care or the responsible continuity team
Pharmacist, nurse educator, dietitian, rehabilitation, mental-health, or social support when relevant to the case.
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer topic-relevant prevention or self-management support that is safe, feasible, culturally appropriate, and consistent with the person’s goals.
Avoid one-size-fits-all restrictions; individualise advice for pregnancy, frailty, kidney/heart disease, disability, and treatment burden.
patientEducation: Explain acute bowel obstruction in plain language, including what is known, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed.
Use teach-back for warning signs, medicines or monitoring, and the route to urgent help.
Invite questions and adapt written or interpreted information to the patient’s language, health literacy, and communication needs.
dischargeCriteria: Clinical status is appropriate for the next setting, and urgent complications have been excluded or addressed.
The patient or caregiver has an understandable plan, access to needed treatment/support, and a clear escalation route.
Pending investigations and referrals have a named owner and follow-up timeframe.

symptoms: Chest pressure, tightness, heaviness, or pain
Discomfort to arm, jaw, back, neck, or upper abdomen
Shortness of breath
Nausea, vomiting, or sweating
Fatigue, lightheadedness, or syncope
physicalSigns: Diaphoresis or pallor
Tachycardia, bradycardia, or arrhythmia
Hypotension or hypertension
Signs of acute heart failure
Examination may be normal

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt severe pain, pulse/BP asymmetry, neurologic deficit, or aortic regurgitation.
Pleuritic pain, unexplained hypoxemia/tachycardia, and VTE risk.
Often positional or pleuritic pain with characteristic ECG changes.
Meal-related, positional, or reproducible features do not alone exclude ACS.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead ECG repeated when symptoms persist/evolve
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG repeated when symptoms persist/evolve — ACS
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Possible ST elevation, ischemic ST depression, T-wave inversion, or dynamic changes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Rapid interpretation guides reperfusion and risk management.

ruleIn.testName: Serial high-sensitivity troponin using local pathway
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial high-sensitivity troponin using local pathway — Acute myocardial injury
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Rise/fall with a value above assay threshold in clinical context.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports diagnosis and risk assessment with symptoms and ECG.

ruleOut.testName: Serial ECG and troponin pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial ECG and troponin pathway — Acute MI
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No evolving ischemic ECG or significant troponin change by validated pathway.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: A single normal ECG or early troponin does not exclude ACS.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when indicated — Alternative thoracic cause or complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No evident pneumothorax, major edema, or other thoracic cause.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assesses selected mimics but does not rule out ACS.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute reduction in coronary blood flow, commonly from plaque disruption and thrombosis, causes myocardial ischemia and may cause infarction.
keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic plaque disruption
Platelet activation and coronary thrombosis
Myocardial oxygen supply-demand imbalance
Myocardial necrosis if ischemia persists

clinicalManagement.title: Rapid assessment and ECG
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, observations, pain, and stability.
Obtain and interpret 12-lead ECG promptly; repeat if symptoms continue or change.
Establish monitoring and IV access; obtain serial biomarkers per local pathway.
Activate local reperfusion pathway and contact cardiology immediately.
Arrange urgent transfer to a reperfusion-capable service.
branches.condition: ST-elevation MI or ongoing high-risk ischemia

actions: Provide resuscitation and urgent senior, cardiology, and critical-care review.
Treat instability per local emergency protocol.
branches.condition: Instability, shock, or malignant arrhythmia

clinicalManagement.title: Initiate protocol-directed ACS care
actions: Administer indicated antiplatelet and other therapies per current Saudi/local protocol after checking contraindications and bleeding risk.
Give oxygen only when indicated by hypoxemia or respiratory distress.
Assess for alternative life-threatening diagnoses before potentially harmful therapies.
Admit or transfer for cardiology-led risk assessment and treatment.
Review ECG, serial troponin, renal function, bleeding risk, and comorbidities.
branches.condition: ACS confirmed or strongly suspected

actions: Evaluate alternative causes and disposition based on overall risk.
Provide return precautions and follow-up.
branches.condition: ACS not established after validated assessment

clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as ACS is suspected

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: For confirmed ACS, arrange cardiology follow-up and cardiac rehabilitation as appropriate.
mdtReferrals: Pharmacy and primary care for medication and risk-factor follow-up
lifestyleAndDiet: Address tobacco, diet, activity, and cardiovascular risks after stabilization.
Support adherence to secondary prevention.
patientEducation: Explain that possible ACS needs urgent assessment even if discomfort improves.
Seek emergency help immediately if symptoms recur.
dischargeCriteria: Assessed by validated ACS pathway
No ongoing instability or unresolved high-risk features
Medication and follow-up plans documented
Emergency return precautions understood

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Assessment and Escalation Pathway

content.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Assessment and Escalation Pathway

redFlags: Persistent or recurrent suspected cardiac chest discomfort
Syncope, shock, pulmonary oedema, or life-threatening arrhythmia
Cardiac arrest or new neurological deficit
symptoms: Chest pressure, tightness, heaviness, or discomfort
Discomfort radiating to arm, shoulder, jaw, back, or upper abdomen
Dyspnoea, nausea, sweating, or unusual fatigue
Atypical or minimal symptoms, especially in older adults and people with diabetes
physicalSigns: Pallor, diaphoresis, or respiratory distress
Tachycardia, bradycardia, hypotension, or irregular pulse
Possible heart-failure signs such as crackles or raised jugular venous pressure

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt severe chest or back pain, pulse or blood-pressure asymmetry, or new aortic regurgitation.
Acute dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxaemia, or venous thromboembolism risk factors.
Often pleuritic or positional pain with compatible ECG findings.
May be meal-related, reflux-associated, movement-related, or reproducible; these features alone do not exclude ACS.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Acute myocardial ischaemia or infarction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: ST elevation or depression, dynamic T-wave change, or another acute ischaemic pattern
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify immediately actionable ischaemia and guide escalation.

ruleIn.testName: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin — Acute myocardial injury
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Rise or fall with at least one value above the assay-specific 99th percentile, interpreted with symptoms and ECG
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detect myocardial injury using symptom timing and the local assay pathway.

ruleIn.testName: Bedside echocardiography when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Bedside echocardiography when indicated — Regional ventricular dysfunction or mechanical complication
ruleIn.expectedFinding: New regional wall-motion abnormality or cardiac dysfunction
ruleIn.targetCondition: Regional ventricular dysfunction or mechanical complication
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess instability or complications when clinically indicated.

ruleOut.testName: Serial 12-lead electrocardiograms
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial 12-lead electrocardiograms — Evolving acute myocardial ischaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No dynamic ischaemic changes during assessment
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Repeat ECG when symptoms persist or recur; one normal ECG does not exclude ACS.

ruleOut.testName: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin using a validated local pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin using a validated local pathway — Acute myocardial infarction
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Values and change below pathway rule-out thresholds with appropriate timing
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Support rule-out only when the complete validated pathway and clinical assessment permit.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when indicated — Selected alternative acute thoracic causes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No finding supporting an alternative such as pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assess relevant alternatives; a normal result does not rule out ACS.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute myocardial ischaemia usually results from reduced coronary blood flow and may progress to infarction, arrhythmia, or haemodynamic compromise.
keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic plaque disruption with platelet activation and thrombosis
Reduced myocardial oxygen supply relative to demand
Progressive myocardial injury

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and stabilisation
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, vital signs, and pain.
Obtain and interpret a 12-lead ECG promptly; repeat for persistent or changing symptoms.
Monitor and establish access according to acuity and local protocol.
Take focused history including onset, risk factors, medicines, allergies, and bleeding risk.
Activate local emergency, cardiology, and reperfusion pathways when indicated.
Begin the relevant resuscitation or emergency stabilisation pathway.
Request immediate senior, critical-care, and cardiology support.
Do not delay escalation for routine investigations.

actions: Escalate urgently for senior assessment and targeted evaluation.
Assess competing diagnoses and contraindications before ACS-directed treatment.
branches.condition: Aortic dissection or another time-critical alternative is suspected

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm working diagnosis and risk
actions: Use serial ECG and biomarker testing under the local validated pathway.
Order blood count, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and other tests as indicated.
Assess haemodynamic status, bleeding risk, comorbidities, and suitability for invasive or reperfusion strategies.

Use the approved ACS protocol and specialist input for treatment decisions.
For discharged patients, document stability, follow-up, and return precautions.
Arrange cardiology and cardiac-rehabilitation follow-up after confirmed ACS.
Continue monitored hospital care and specialist-led management.
Document receiving team and structured handover.

actions: Provide a documented explanation and follow-up plan.
Advise emergency reassessment for recurrent or worsening symptoms.
branches.condition: ACS excluded through local pathway and no emergency alternative suspected

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange follow-up for the final diagnosis; confirmed ACS requires a documented cardiology and cardiac-rehabilitation plan.

patientEducation: Explain urgent ECGs, blood tests, monitoring, and possible transfer.
Discuss warning symptoms requiring emergency reassessment.
For confirmed ACS, explain follow-up and prescribed risk-reduction plan.
dischargeCriteria: Time-critical causes have been assessed using an appropriate pathway.
Patient is clinically stable and disposition is documented.
Follow-up instructions and return precautions are communicated.
